# Evidence Library screening + synthesis (v2)

You screen sports-science PDFs and, if eligible, write a library record for Baylor Athletics performance, medical, rehab, nutrition and research staff.

Inputs: `inputs.json` gives each paper an ID, the filename it was catalogued under (`sourceFile`), page count, and DOI strings found anywhere in the text (`doiCandidatesInText`; most are from the reference list). Full extracted text is at `text/<ID>.txt`. Read it fully, in chunks if large. Controlled vocabularies are in `taxonomy.json`. Use ONLY those exact values. Base everything ONLY on the extracted text, never on outside knowledge of the paper.

## Decision
- `INCLUDE`: the text is the article the filename names, AND it is athlete health/performance evidence of one of these types: original research (any design, including case reports and validation studies), systematic review/meta-analysis, narrative or clinical review, or consensus/position statement.
- `EXCLUDE` (give `exclusionReason`):
  - (a) source identity mismatch: the text is a different article from what the filename names. Compare the filename title with the title in the text carefully.
  - (b) editorial, commentary, letter, or opinion piece without original methods or a structured review of evidence. Also (b): a study protocol with no results (decided by Eric 2026-10-10; no listed reason fits exactly, so use (b) and say "study protocol, no results" in the reason).
  - (c) not relevant to athletes, sport, exercise performance or athlete health.
- `DEGRADED` (give `degradedReason`): the text is unreadable or truncated, critical sections are missing, or **the article's own DOI is not printed in the text**. Reference-list DOIs do not count. If the DOI is missing but everything else is fine, still fill in all fields and set `doiMissing: true`. The operator may verify the DOI externally and upgrade the decision.

## Output: write `drafts/<ID>.json`
```
{
 "id":"<ID>", "sourceFile":"...", "decision":"INCLUDE|EXCLUDE|DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"one sentence: title found in text vs filename",
 "confidence":"high|medium|low",
 "studyDesign":"<one studyDesigns value>",
 "primaryDomain":"<one domains value>", "domains":[...must include primaryDomain], "audiences":[...], "sports":[...], "populations":[...],
 "evidenceSummary":"2-3 sentences: design, sample, main results, as the authors report them",
 "screeningLimitations":"1-2 sentences: key limits on what this evidence can support",
 "synthesisCaution":"1 sentence: the most likely way staff could over-read this paper",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020, "citation":"Authors. Title. Journal. Year;vol(issue):pages.", "doi":"10.xxxx/...",
   "abstract":"", "tldr":"", "methods":"", "findings":"", "limitations":"",
   "practicalImplications":"", "athleteDev":"", "rtp":""
 }
}
```
For EXCLUDE, the taxonomy, summary and `paper` fields may be null.

## Field rules
- `year`: the journal issue/publication year from the citation line or the journal header. NOT the received, accepted or online-first date. If only an online-first date exists, use that year.
- `doi`: the article's own DOI, exactly as printed, lowercase prefix "10.". Never use a DOI from the references.
- `citation`: list authors as printed (surname + initials; use "et al." after 6 authors). Include volume, issue and pages only if they are printed for this article. Do not invent them.
- `populations`: add `Male Athletes` and/or `Female Athletes` when the sample is athletes and their sex is stated. Do not use athlete tags (sex or `Healthy Athletes`) for non-athlete samples such as recreationally active adults, patients, staff or students; use `Adult / Recreational` or `Mixed / Unspecified`. Add `Healthy Athletes` or `Injured Athletes` when health status is stated. Add the competition level (Professional / Elite, Collegiate, Youth / Adolescent, Adult / Recreational). Use `Mixed / Unspecified` only when the level really is mixed or unstated.
- `studyDesign`: code scoping reviews with a described systematic search as `Systematic Review / Meta-analysis` (library precedent). Use `Narrative Review` only when no search method is described.
- `primaryDomain`: the domain staff would browse to find this paper. Use Monitoring & Technology for papers whose main contribution is a measurement tool, test, device or monitoring method, including reliability, validity and test profiling.
- If the abstract and the results/tables disagree, report the results/table values and note the conflict in `limitations`.

## Writing standard (critical)
- Every claim must be directly supported by the text. Report sample sizes, designs, effect directions and significance accurately. Never invent numbers.
- Distinguish within-group change from between-group difference. Distinguish association from causation. Do not overstate observational or small-sample findings.
- Each paper field: 1-3 plain sentences. `tldr`: one or two practitioner sentences. `athleteDev` = Performance Application. `rtp` = Return to Sport Application. If the study cannot inform return to sport, say what it cannot be used for.
- Practical fields must follow from the findings. No generic advice the paper does not support.
- Plain language, no em dashes.

## Files
Write only to `drafts/<ID>.json` and your own `helpers/<your-folder>/`. Never write anywhere else, including the filesystem root.

# Evidence Library screening + synthesis (v2)

You screen sports-science PDFs and, if eligible, write a library record for Baylor Athletics performance, medical, rehab, nutrition and research staff.

Inputs: `inputs.json` gives each paper an ID, the filename it was catalogued under (`sourceFile`), page count, and DOI strings found anywhere in the text (`doiCandidatesInText`; most are from the reference list). Full extracted text is at `text/<ID>.txt`. Read it fully, in chunks if large. Controlled vocabularies are in `taxonomy.json`. Use ONLY those exact values. Base everything ONLY on the extracted text, never on outside knowledge of the paper.

## Decision
- `INCLUDE`: the text is the article the filename names, AND it is athlete health/performance evidence of one of these types: original research (any design, including case reports and validation studies), systematic review/meta-analysis, narrative or clinical review, or consensus/position statement.
- `EXCLUDE` (give `exclusionReason`):
  - (a) source identity mismatch: the text is a different article from what the filename names. Compare the filename title with the title in the text carefully.
  - (b) editorial, commentary, letter, or opinion piece without original methods or a structured review of evidence. Also (b): a study protocol with no results (decided by Eric 2026-10-10; no listed reason fits exactly, so use (b) and say "study protocol, no results" in the reason).
  - (c) not relevant to athletes, sport, exercise performance or athlete health.
- `DEGRADED` (give `degradedReason`): the text is unreadable or truncated, critical sections are missing, or **the article's own DOI is not printed in the text**. Reference-list DOIs do not count. If the DOI is missing but everything else is fine, still fill in all fields and set `doiMissing: true`. The operator may verify the DOI externally and upgrade the decision.

## Output: write `drafts/<ID>.json`
```
{
 "id":"<ID>", "sourceFile":"...", "decision":"INCLUDE|EXCLUDE|DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"one sentence: title found in text vs filename",
 "confidence":"high|medium|low",
 "studyDesign":"<one studyDesigns value>",
 "primaryDomain":"<one domains value>", "domains":[...must include primaryDomain], "audiences":[...], "sports":[...], "populations":[...],
 "evidenceSummary":"2-3 sentences: design, sample, main results, as the authors report them",
 "screeningLimitations":"1-2 sentences: key limits on what this evidence can support",
 "synthesisCaution":"1 sentence: the most likely way staff could over-read this paper",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020, "citation":"Authors. Title. Journal. Year;vol(issue):pages.", "doi":"10.xxxx/...",
   "abstract":"", "tldr":"", "methods":"", "findings":"", "limitations":"",
   "practicalImplications":"", "athleteDev":"", "rtp":""
 }
}
```
For EXCLUDE, the taxonomy, summary and `paper` fields may be null.

## Field rules
- `year`: the journal issue/publication year from the citation line or the journal header. NOT the received, accepted or online-first date. If only an online-first date exists, use that year.
- `doi`: the article's own DOI, exactly as printed, lowercase prefix "10.". Never use a DOI from the references.
- `citation`: list authors as printed (surname + initials; use "et al." after 6 authors). Include volume, issue and pages only if they are printed for this article. Do not invent them.
- `populations`: add `Male Athletes` and/or `Female Athletes` when the sample is athletes and their sex is stated. Do not use athlete tags (sex or `Healthy Athletes`) for non-athlete samples such as recreationally active adults, patients, staff or students; use `Adult / Recreational` or `Mixed / Unspecified`. Add `Healthy Athletes` or `Injured Athletes` when health status is stated. Add the competition level (Professional / Elite, Collegiate, Youth / Adolescent, Adult / Recreational). Use `Mixed / Unspecified` only when the level really is mixed or unstated.
- `studyDesign`: code scoping reviews with a described systematic search as `Systematic Review / Meta-analysis` (library precedent). Use `Narrative Review` only when no search method is described.
- `primaryDomain`: the domain staff would browse to find this paper. Use Monitoring & Technology for papers whose main contribution is a measurement tool, test, device or monitoring method, including reliability, validity and test profiling.
- If the abstract and the results/tables disagree, report the results/table values and note the conflict in `limitations`.

## Writing standard (critical)
- Every claim must be directly supported by the text. Report sample sizes, designs, effect directions and significance accurately. Never invent numbers.
- Distinguish within-group change from between-group difference. Distinguish association from causation. Do not overstate observational or small-sample findings.
- Each paper field: 1-3 plain sentences. `tldr`: one or two practitioner sentences. `athleteDev` = Performance Application. `rtp` = Return to Sport Application. If the study cannot inform return to sport, say what it cannot be used for.
- Practical fields must follow from the findings. No generic advice the paper does not support.
- Plain language, no em dashes.

## Files
Write only to `drafts/<ID>.json` and your own `helpers/<your-folder>/`. Never write anywhere else, including the filesystem root.

15	  Objective: This study summarizes findings from a cross-sectional survey conducted among National Collegiate Athletic Asso-
16	  ciation (NCAA) Division 1 football programs, focusing on sport-related concussion (SRC) protocols for the 2018 season. Design:
17	  Cross-sectional survey study. Setting: 65 football programs within the Autonomy Five (A5) NCAA conferences. Participants:
18	  Athletic trainers and team physicians who attended a football safety meeting at the NCAA offices June 17 to 18, 2019, representing
19	  their respective institutions. Intervention: Electronic surveys were distributed on June 14, 2019, before the football safety
20	  meeting. Main Outcome Measures: Results for 16 unique questions involving SRC protocols and resources were summa-
21	  rized and evaluated. Results: The survey garnered responses from 46 of 65 programs (response rate 5 71%). For baseline testing,
22	  98% measured baseline postural stability and balance, 87% used baseline neurocognitive testing, while only 61% assessed
23	  baseline vestibular and/or ocular function. Regarding concussion prevention, 51% did not recommend additional measures, while
24	  4% and 24% recommended cervical compression collars and omega-3 supplementation, respectively. In postconcussion treat-
25	  ment, 26% initiated aerobic exercise 1 day postconcussion if symptoms were stable, 24% waited at least 48 hours, 4% waited for
26	  the athlete to return to baseline, 11% waited until the athlete became asymptomatic, and 35% determined procedures on a case-
27	  by-case basis. Conclusions: Most institutions assessed postural stability/balance and neurocognitive functioning at baseline
28	  and introduced light aerobic exercise within 48 h postconcussion. There was variation in baseline assessment methods and
29	  concussion prevention recommendations. These survey findings deepen our understanding of diverse SRC protocols in NCAA
30	  football programs.
31	  Key Words: sport-related concussion, football, universities, survey

Original Research




What are the Protocols and Resources for
Sport-Related Concussion Among Top National
Collegiate Athletic Association Football Programs?
A Cross-Sectional Survey of A5 Schools
James R. Clugston, MD,*† Kelsey Diemer, DO,* Sarah L. Chrabaszcz, MD,‡§ Connor C. Long, BS,{
Jacob Jo, BA,║** Douglas P. Terry, PhD,** Scott L. Zuckerman, MD, MPH,** and Robert Warne Fitch, MD††‡‡


  Abstract
  Objective: This study summarizes findings from a cross-sectional survey conducted among National Collegiate Athletic Asso-
  ciation (NCAA) Division 1 football programs, focusing on sport-related concussion (SRC) protocols for the 2018 season. Design:
  Cross-sectional survey study. Setting: 65 football programs within the Autonomy Five (A5) NCAA conferences. Participants:
  Athletic trainers and team physicians who attended a football safety meeting at the NCAA offices June 17 to 18, 2019, representing
  their respective institutions. Intervention: Electronic surveys were distributed on June 14, 2019, before the football safety
  meeting. Main Outcome Measures: Results for 16 unique questions involving SRC protocols and resources were summa-
  rized and evaluated. Results: The survey garnered responses from 46 of 65 programs (response rate 5 71%). For baseline testing,
  98% measured baseline postural stability and balance, 87% used baseline neurocognitive testing, while only 61% assessed
  baseline vestibular and/or ocular function. Regarding concussion prevention, 51% did not recommend additional measures, while
  4% and 24% recommended cervical compression collars and omega-3 supplementation, respectively. In postconcussion treat-
  ment, 26% initiated aerobic exercise 1 day postconcussion if symptoms were stable, 24% waited at least 48 hours, 4% waited for
  the athlete to return to baseline, 11% waited until the athlete became asymptomatic, and 35% determined procedures on a case-
  by-case basis. Conclusions: Most institutions assessed postural stability/balance and neurocognitive functioning at baseline
  and introduced light aerobic exercise within 48 h postconcussion. There was variation in baseline assessment methods and
  concussion prevention recommendations. These survey findings deepen our understanding of diverse SRC protocols in NCAA
  football programs.
  Key Words: sport-related concussion, football, universities, survey
  (Clin J Sport Med 2024;00:1–7)

{
 "id": "Q60",
 "sourceFile": "Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness - A narrative review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness: A narrative review' matches the filename title.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A narrative review, built from a PubMed and ScienceDirect search (June 2023) that retained 15 articles: nine on ingestible core temperature capsules, four on wearable core temperature estimation, and two on wearable prediction of exertional heat stroke (EHS). Ingestible capsules showed small mean biases against rectal temperature (for example 0.13 +/- 0.26 C and 0.15 C), with variability that increased after exercise, while the four wearable core-temperature studies reported unacceptable limits of agreement. In the two EHS prediction studies, one device-plus-gait approach identified all six EHS casualties 3.5 minutes before collapse with a 6.1% false-positive rate (n = 209), and another wearable had 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The search covered only PubMed and ScienceDirect, in English, and no formal quality appraisal is described, so the 15 included articles are not a complete or graded evidence base. The authors label the paper a narrative review; the design code follows the taxonomy rule that a described search method is coded as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the ingestible capsule validity data as proof that capsules or wearables prevent or detect heat illness, when the review found the wearable EHS evidence rests on two studies and no wearable was validated for core temperature during activity in the heat.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Hintz CN, Butler CR. Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness: A narrative review. PM&R. 2024;1-6.",
   "doi": "10.1002/pmrj.13155",
   "abstract": "This narrative review examines wearable and ingestible technology that estimates core temperature to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness (EHI) in athletes, military members and laborers. The authors find few data on the accuracy of newer wearable devices during true heat stroke physiology and caution against overreliance on these devices. They argue that accuracy and real-world diagnostic value must be proven, and that education and prevention policy remain the main tools.",
   "tldr": "Ingestible capsules track core temperature reasonably well against rectal readings, but wearable devices have not been validated for core temperature during activity in the heat. Use them as a supplement to education and prevention, not as a stand-alone screen for heat illness.",
   "methods": "A narrative review using a PubMed and ScienceDirect search (June 23, 2023) with terms for wearable or ingestible technology, exertional heat illness and military, sports or workforce settings, with no date limit. Studies had to estimate core temperature noninvasively or ingestibly against a rectal, GI or telemetry reference; 75 articles were screened down to 15 (nine ingestible, four wearable core-temperature, two wearable EHS prediction).",
   "findings": "Ingestible capsules showed mean differences from rectal temperature of 0.13 +/- 0.26 C (Teunissen) and 0.15 C (Gant), and capsule-to-capsule discordance widened from -0.40 to +0.42 C at rest to -0.86 to +0.68 C after activity. Post-2022 wearable core-temperature studies all reported unacceptable limits of agreement. For EHS, one study found all six casualties 3.5 minutes before collapse with a 6.1% false-positive rate (n = 209), while another reported 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.",
   "limitations": "The review is limited by its search of two databases, English-only inclusion and the absence of a described quality appraisal. Its conclusions rest on a small number of EHS prediction studies, and the authors acknowledge that wearable accuracy may fall with body composition, movement, clothing and sweat. No abstract-to-results conflict was found.",
   "practicalImplications": "A team using ingestible capsules should calibrate them, plan ingestion so the capsule is still in the gut when needed, and budget for single-use capsules and a recorder within about 2 feet of the athlete. Wearables should not replace education on EHI signs, acclimation, WBGT monitoring, work-rest cycles, hydration and rapid cooling, and flagged athletes need clinical review rather than reliance on the device alone.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Core temperature estimates may help track heat strain during training, but the review found that none of the wearable or ingestible devices had been validated for core temperature during activity in the heat, so any training decision based on them needs local validation first.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: This review is not a return-to-sport study and cannot establish when an athlete recovering from exertional heat illness is safe to return. It does support not clearing an athlete on a wearable reading alone, because the authors warn that device estimates can give false reassurance."
 }
}

   "abstract": "This narrative review examines wearable and ingestible technology that estimates core temperature to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness (EHI) in athletes, military members and laborers. The authors find few data on the accuracy of newer wearable devices during true heat stroke physiology and caution against overreliance on these devices. They argue that accuracy and real-world diagnostic value must be proven, and that education and prevention policy remain the main tools.",
   "tldr": "Ingestible capsules track core temperature reasonably well against rectal readings, but wearable devices have not been validated for core temperature during activity in the heat. Use them as a supplement to education and prevention, not as a stand-alone screen for heat illness.",
   "methods": "A narrative review using a PubMed and ScienceDirect search (June 23, 2023) with terms for wearable or ingestible technology, exertional heat illness and military, sports or workforce settings, with no date limit. Studies had to estimate core temperature noninvasively or ingestibly against a rectal, GI or telemetry reference; 75 articles were screened down to 15 (nine ingestible, four wearable core-temperature, two wearable EHS prediction).",
   "findings": "Ingestible capsules showed mean differences from rectal temperature of 0.13 +/- 0.26 C (Teunissen) and 0.15 C (Gant), and capsule-to-capsule discordance widened from -0.40 to +0.42 C at rest to -0.86 to +0.68 C after activity. Post-2022 wearable core-temperature studies all reported unacceptable limits of agreement. For EHS, one study found all six casualties 3.5 minutes before collapse with a 6.1% false-positive rate (n = 209), while another reported 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.",
   "limitations": "The review is limited by its search of two databases, English-only inclusion and the absence of a described quality appraisal. Its conclusions rest on a small number of EHS prediction studies, and the authors acknowledge that wearable accuracy may fall with body composition, movement, clothing and sweat. No abstract-to-results conflict was found.",
   "practicalImplications": "A team using ingestible capsules should calibrate them, plan ingestion so the capsule is still in the gut when needed, and budget for single-use capsules and a recorder within about 2 feet of the athlete.    "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Core temperature estimates may help track heat strain during training, but the review found that none of the wearable or ingestible devices had been validated for core temperature during activity in the heat, so any training decision based on them needs local validation first.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: This review is not a return-to-sport study and cannot establish when an athlete recovering from exertional heat illness is safe to return. Group, USAF, San Antonio, Texas, USA
                                                    Exertional heat illness remains a constant threat to the athlete, military service
Correspondence

Courtney N. Hintz, Special Warfare Human            ronmental heat waves places these populations at an ever increasing risk and

Email: courtney.hintz.1@us.af.mil                   and laborers in the implementation of awareness, education, and measures to
                                                    reduce or mitigate the risk of exertional heat illness. Within the past 2 decades,
                                                    a variety of wearable technology options have become commercially available
                                                    to track an estimation of core temperature, yet questions continue to emerge
                                                    as to its use, effectiveness, and practicality in athletics, the military, and the
                                                    workforce. There is a paucity of data on the accuracy of many of these newer
                                                    devices in the setting of true heat stroke physiology, and it is important to
                                                    avoid overreliance on new wearable technology. Further research and
                                                    improvement of this technology are critical to identify accuracy in the diagno-
                                                    sis and prevention of EHI.

{
 "id": "Q60",
 "sourceFile": "Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness - A narrative review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness: A narrative review' matches the filename title.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A narrative review, built from a PubMed and ScienceDirect search (June 2023) that retained 15 articles: nine on ingestible core temperature capsules, four on wearable core temperature estimation, and two on wearable prediction of exertional heat stroke (EHS). Ingestible capsules showed small mean biases against rectal temperature (for example 0.13 +/- 0.26 C and 0.15 C), with variability that increased after exercise, while the four wearable core-temperature studies reported unacceptable limits of agreement. In the two EHS prediction studies, one device-plus-gait approach identified all six EHS casualties 3.5 minutes before collapse with a 6.1% false-positive rate (n = 209), and another wearable had 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The search covered only PubMed and ScienceDirect, in English, and no formal quality appraisal is described, so the 15 included articles are not a complete or graded evidence base. The authors label the paper a narrative review; the design code follows the taxonomy rule that a described search method is coded as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the capsule validity data or wearable marketing as proof that these devices detect or prevent heat illness, when the review found the wearable EHS evidence rests on two studies (one with 20% sensitivity) and recent wearable core-temperature studies all showed unacceptable limits of agreement.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Hintz CN, Butler CR. Wearable and ingestible technology to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness: A narrative review. PM&R. 2024;1-6.",
   "doi": "10.1002/pmrj.13155",
   "abstract": "This narrative review examines wearable and ingestible technology that estimates core temperature to evaluate and prevent exertional heat illness (EHI) in athletes, military members and laborers. The authors find few data on the accuracy of newer wearable devices during true heat stroke physiology and caution against overreliance on these devices. They argue that accuracy and real-world diagnostic value must be proven, and that education and prevention policy remain the main tools.",
   "tldr": "Ingestible capsules track core temperature reasonably well against rectal readings, but wearable core-temperature estimates showed unacceptable agreement and have little evidence for detecting real heat stroke. Use them as a supplement to education and prevention, not as a stand-alone screen for heat illness.",
   "methods": "A narrative review using a PubMed and ScienceDirect search (June 23, 2023) with terms for wearable or ingestible technology, exertional heat illness and military, sports or workforce settings, with no date limit. Studies had to estimate core temperature noninvasively or ingestibly against a rectal, GI or telemetry reference; 75 articles were screened down to 15 (nine ingestible, four wearable core-temperature, two wearable EHS prediction).",
   "findings": "Ingestible capsules showed mean differences from rectal temperature of 0.13 +/- 0.26 C (Teunissen) and 0.15 C (Gant), and capsule-to-capsule discordance widened from -0.40 to +0.42 C at rest to -0.86 to +0.68 C after activity. Post-2022 wearable core-temperature studies all reported unacceptable limits of agreement. For EHS, one study found all six casualties 3.5 minutes before collapse with a 6.1% false-positive rate (n = 209), while another reported 20% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.",
   "limitations": "The review is limited by its search of two databases, English-only inclusion and the absence of a described quality appraisal. Its conclusions rest on a small number of EHS prediction studies, and the authors acknowledge that wearable accuracy may fall with body composition, movement, clothing and sweat. No abstract-to-results conflict was found.",
   "practicalImplications": "A team using ingestible capsules should calibrate them, plan ingestion so the capsule is still in the gut when needed, and budget for single-use capsules and a recorder within about 2 feet of the athlete. Wearables should not replace education on EHI signs, acclimation, WBGT monitoring, work-rest cycles, hydration and rapid cooling, and flagged athletes need clinical review rather than reliance on the device alone.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Ingestible capsules can track core temperature during training in the heat once calibrated, but wearable core-temperature estimates showed unacceptable agreement with reference measures, so any training decision based on a wearable needs local validation first.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: This review is not a return-to-sport study and cannot establish when an athlete recovering from exertional heat illness is safe to return. It does support not clearing an athlete on a wearable reading alone, because the authors warn that device estimates can give false reassurance."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status": "CORRECTED",
   "changes": [
     "paper.athleteDev: said none of the wearable or ingestible devices were validated in the heat -> ingestible capsules were judged valid; wearables showed unacceptable agreement ('the temperature variability in ingestible devices is low enough to warrant use to track core temperature')",
     "paper.tldr: 'wearable devices have not been validated for core temperature during activity in the heat' -> wearable estimates showed unacceptable agreement (the 'none validated' line refers only to consumer devices such as the Oura ring, Fitbit and Apple Watch)",
     "synthesisCaution: same overgeneralization about all wearables -> reframed on the two EHS studies and the unacceptable limits of agreement ('all manuscripts identifying unacceptable limits of agreement')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns": "Heat illness is safety-critical. One of the two EHS prediction studies (Hintz 2023) is the first author's own work. Minus signs on capsule biases appear lost in text extraction, so bias direction is reported as magnitude only.",
   "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Research & Analytics", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "This retrospective team-level analysis of the 2015-2019 NFL regular seasons compared games missed, Football Outsiders' AGL, a new position-weighted metric (wAGL, weighted by 2019 franchise-tag values) and a player-weighted metric (WAIL, based on PFF WAR). Each metric was correlated with the gap between end-of-season and preseason-projected DVOA and win totals. wAGL had the strongest correlations (r = -0.37 with the DVOA difference and -0.38 with the win difference), compared with -0.32 and -0.35 for AGL, -0.35 and -0.35 for games missed, and -0.18 and -0.19 for WAIL.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The outcome used as the gold standard is a proxy (preseason projections versus actual results), which the authors themselves describe as likely flawed, and the correlations are modest with no confidence intervals or significance tests reported. The evidence covers one league at the team level over five seasons, relies on public injury reports that can understate injury incidence, and the wAGL reserve weight (R = 0.6) was chosen by maximizing correlation with the same outcome.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read wAGL as a validated measure of what an injury costs any team or sport, when it was tested only on NFL team outcomes using 2019 franchise-tag weights.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Glazer A, Binney Z, Seth T. Weighted Approaches to Assessing Injury Burden in Team Sports. Journal of Sports Analytics. 2025;10(4):1-9.",
   "doi": "10.1177/22150218241304941",
   "abstract": "The authors compare games missed, AGL, a position-weighted metric (wAGL) and a player-weighted metric (WAIL) as measures of NFL team injury burden. Each measure was tested against the gap between actual and preseason-projected team performance and wins across the 2015-2019 seasons. wAGL was the strongest of the measures tested, and WAIL was the weakest.",
   "tldr": "When the question is how injuries affect team results, weighting each injury by its position's value (wAGL) tracked those results better than counting games lost or using unweighted AGL. The player-level WAIL metric tracked them worst, so the weighting method matters.",
   "methods": "Team-level analysis of NFL regular seasons from 2015-2019, with 2020-2021 excluded because of COVID-19. Metrics were AGL, wAGL (AGL weighted by 2019 franchise-tag position values, with reserve players counted at 0.6 of a starter), WAIL (games missed weighted by PFF WAR-Adjusted Injuries Lost) and a simple count of games missed. Each was correlated with the difference between actual and preseason-projected DVOA and win totals, and a sensitivity analysis doubled the QB weight in wAGL.",
   "findings": "wAGL had the strongest correlation with both outcomes: r = -0.37 with the DVOA difference and -0.38 with the win difference. AGL gave -0.32 and -0.35, games missed gave -0.35 and -0.35, and WAIL gave -0.18 and -0.19. Doubling the QB weight raised wAGL to -0.39 and -0.40, and wAGL and AGL correlated 0.92 with each other. These are associations with a proxy outcome rather than causal effects, and the differences between metrics are small.",
   "limitations": "The text and tables conflict in two places: the prose gives the 2015-2019 wAGL standard deviation as 26.5 while the Table 4 caption gives 36.5, and the appendix text says franchise-tag weights outperform the alternatives while Table 6 shows the Clay weights slightly higher (-0.38 and -0.39 versus -0.37 and -0.38). No p-values or confidence intervals are reported, and the gold standard is a proxy that the authors call likely flawed. Public injury reports can understate incidence, in-game departures were not captured, and the QB-weight sensitivity result was added after the main analysis.",
   "practicalImplications": "For questions about how injuries affect team results, a position-weighted measure such as wAGL can be used alongside a count of games missed. For questions about whether a rule or prevention program reduces injuries, the authors recommend plain counts of games missed or injuries instead. The weights are NFL-specific, and the authors' view that the concept extends to other sports was not tested.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the paper's logic only when the question is about team-level impact, since the authors recommend plain counts for descriptive injury questions. The franchise-tag weights are NFL-specific and would need to be rebuilt before use with another league or roster structure.",
   "rtp": "This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It is a team-season metric built from public injury report designations and preseason projections, with no individual recovery, readiness or clearance data."
 }
}

Abstract
Injuries have a large impact on a team’s success during the season. Typically teams with more injuries, especially those
affecting the most valuable players, will perform worse than similar teams with fewer injuries. A common way to quantify
a team’s injury burden is by simply counting the number of injuries or games missed due to injury. However, these mea-
sures do not account for the individual value of the players injured. We assess two frameworks for how injuries may be
weighted by player value. We propose a new position-weighted metric based on franchise tag values to measure injury
burden in American football, called weighted Adjusted Games Lost (wAGL), and we test another player-level metric,
Wins Above Replacement-Adjusted Injuries Lost (WAIL). WAIL uses a proprietary calculation of player Wins Above
Replacement from Pro Football Focus. By comparing these measures to a gold standard of injury burden using pre- versus
end-season betting lines and team strength estimates, we ﬁnd that wAGL is a better measure of injury burden than cur-
rent alternatives across all team-seasons considered.

content.content:
The text and tables conflict in two places: the prose gives the 2015-2019 wAGL standard deviation as 26.5 while the Table 4 caption gives 36.5, and the appendix text says franchise-tag weights outperform the alternatives while Table 6 shows the Clay weights slightly higher (-0.38 and -0.39 versus -0.37 and -0.38). No p-values or confidence intervals are reported, and the gold standard is a proxy that the authors call likely flawed. Public injury reports can understate incidence, in-game departures were not captured, and the QB-doubled wAGL variant was tuned on the same outcomes it was evaluated against.

 }

What Role Do Chronic Workloads Play in the Acute to Chronic
Workload Ratio? Time to Dismiss ACWR and Its Underlying Theory
Franco M. Impellizzeri1         · S. Woodcock2 · A. J. Coutts1 · M. Fanchini3 · A. McCall4 · A. D. Vigotsky5,6

Accepted: 23 October 2020
© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020


Abstract
Aim The aim of this study was to examine the associations between the injury risk and the acute (AL) to chronic (CL)
workload ratio (ACWR) by substituting the original CL with contrived values to assess the role of CL (i.e., the presence and
implications of statistical artefacts).
Methods Using previously published data, we generated a contrived ACWR by dividing the AL by fixed and randomly
generated CLs, and we compared these results to real data. We also reproduced previously reported subgroup analyses,
including dichotomising players’ data above and below the median CL. Our analyses follow the same, previously published
modelling approach.
Results The analyses with original data showed effects compatible with higher injury risk for ACWR only (odd ratios,
OR: 2.45, 95% CI 1.28–4.71). However, we observed similar effects by dividing AL by the “contrived” fixed and randomly
generated CLs: OR 1.95 (1.18–3.52) dividing by 1510 (average CL); and OR ranging from 1.16 to 2.07, using random CL
1.53 (mean). Random ACWRs reduced the variance relative to the original AL and further inflated the ORs (mean OR 1.89,
from 1.42 to 2.70). ACWR causes artificial reclassification of players compared to AL alone. Finally, neither ACWR nor
AL alone confer a meaningful predictive advantage to an intercept-only model, even within the training sample (c-statistic
0.574/0.544 vs. 0.5 in both ACWR/AL and intercept-only models, respectively).
Discussion ACWR is a rescaling of the explanatory variable (AL, numerator), in turn magnifying its effect estimates and
decreasing its variance despite conferring no predictive advantage. Other ratio-related transformations (e.g., reducing the
variance of the explanatory variable and unjustified reclassifications) further inflate the OR of AL alone with injury risk.
These results also disprove the etiological theory behind this ratio and its components. We suggest ACWR be dismissed as
a framework and model, and in line with this, injury frameworks, recommendations, and consensus be updated to reflect the
lack of predictive value of and statistical artefacts inherent in ACWR models.

9	A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map from 300 Trials
10	José Afonso1 · Renato Andrade2,3,4 · Sílvia Rocha‑Rodrigues5,6,10 · Fábio Yuzo Nakamura7 · Hugo Sarmento8 ·

18	Abstract
19	Background Stretching has garnered significant attention in sports sciences, resulting in numerous studies. However, there
20	is no comprehensive overview on investigation of stretching in healthy athletes.
21	Objectives To perform a systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map of stretching studies in healthy athletes,
22	identify current gaps in the literature, and provide stakeholders with priorities for future research.
23	Methods Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guide-
24	lines were followed. We included studies comprising healthy athletes exposed to acute and/or chronic stretching interventions.
25	Six databases were searched (CINAHL, EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science) until 1 January
26	2023. The relevant data were narratively synthesized; quantitative data summaries were provided for key data items. An
27	evidence gap map was developed to offer an overview of the existing research and relevant gaps.
28	Results Of ~ 220,000 screened records, we included 300 trials involving 7080 athletes [mostly males (~ 65% versus ~ 20%
29	female, and ~ 15% unreported) under 36 years of age; tiers 2 and 3 of the Participant Classification Framework] across
30	43 sports. Sports requiring extreme range of motion (e.g., gymnastics) were underrepresented. Most trials assessed the
31	acute effects of stretching, with chronic effects being scrutinized in less than 20% of trials. Chronic interventions averaged
32	7.4 ± 5.1 weeks and never exceeded 6 months. Most trials (~ 85%) implemented stretching within the warm-up, with other
33	application timings (e.g., post-exercise) being under-researched. Most trials examined static active stretching (62.3%), fol-
34	lowed by dynamic stretching (38.3%) and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) stretching (12.0%), with scarce
35	research on alternative methods (e.g., ballistic stretching). Comparators were mostly limited to passive controls, with ~ 25%
36	of trials including active controls (e.g., strength training). The lower limbs were primarily targeted by interventions (~ 75%).
37	Reporting of dose was heterogeneous in style (e.g., 10 repetitions versus 10 s for dynamic stretching) and completeness
38	of information (i.e., with disparities in the comprehensiveness of the provided information). Most trials (~ 90%) reported
39	performance-related outcomes (mainly strength/power and range of motion); sport-specific outcomes were collected in less
40	than 15% of trials. Biomechanical, physiological, and neural/psychological outcomes were assessed sparsely and heteroge-
41	neously; only five trials investigated injury-related outcomes.
42	Conclusions There is room for improvement, with many areas of research on stretching being underexplored and others cur-
43	rently too heterogeneous for reliable comparisons between studies. There is limited representation of elite-level athletes (~ 5%
44	tier 4 and no tier 5) and underpowered sample sizes (≤ 20 participants). Research was biased toward adult male athletes of
45	sports not requiring extreme ranges of motion, and mostly assessed the acute effects of static active stretching and dynamic
46	stretching during the warm-up. Dose–response relationships remain largely underexplored. Outcomes were mostly limited
47	to general performance testing. Injury prevention and other effects of stretching remain poorly investigated. These relevant
48	research gaps should be prioritized by funding policies.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



What We Do Not Know About Stretching in Healthy Athletes:
A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map from 300 Trials
José Afonso1 · Renato Andrade2,3,4 · Sílvia Rocha‑Rodrigues5,6,10 · Fábio Yuzo Nakamura7 · Hugo Sarmento8 ·
Sandro R. Freitas9 · Ana Filipa Silva5,10 · Lorenzo Laporta11 · Maryam Abarghoueinejad12 · Zeki Akyildiz13 ·
Rongzhi Chen1 · Andreia Pizarro14,15 · Rodrigo Ramirez‑Campillo16 · Filipe Manuel Clemente5,10,17

Accepted: 3 February 2024
© The Author(s) 2024


Abstract
Background Stretching has garnered significant attention in sports sciences, resulting in numerous studies. However, there
is no comprehensive overview on investigation of stretching in healthy athletes.
Objectives To perform a systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map of stretching studies in healthy athletes,
identify current gaps in the literature, and provide stakeholders with priorities for future research.
Methods Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guide-
lines were followed. We included studies comprising healthy athletes exposed to acute and/or chronic stretching interventions.
Six databases were searched (CINAHL, EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science) until 1 January
2023. The relevant data were narratively synthesized; quantitative data summaries were provided for key data items. An
evidence gap map was developed to offer an overview of the existing research and relevant gaps.
Results Of ~ 220,000 screened records, we included 300 trials involving 7080 athletes [mostly males (~ 65% versus ~ 20%
female, and ~ 15% unreported) under 36 years of age; tiers 2 and 3 of the Participant Classification Framework] across
43 sports. Sports requiring extreme range of motion (e.g., gymnastics) were underrepresented. Most trials assessed the
acute effects of stretching, with chronic effects being scrutinized in less than 20% of trials. Chronic interventions averaged
7.4 ± 5.1 weeks and never exceeded 6 months. Most trials (~ 85%) implemented stretching within the warm-up, with other
application timings (e.g., post-exercise) being under-researched. Most trials examined static active stretching (62.3%), fol-
lowed by dynamic stretching (38.3%) and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) stretching (12.0%), with scarce
research on alternative methods (e.g., ballistic stretching). Comparators were mostly limited to passive controls, with ~ 25%
of trials including active controls (e.g., strength training). The lower limbs were primarily targeted by interventions (~ 75%).
Reporting of dose was heterogeneous in style (e.g., 10 repetitions versus 10 s for dynamic stretching) and completeness
of information (i.e., with disparities in the comprehensiveness of the provided information). Most trials (~ 90%) reported
performance-related outcomes (mainly strength/power and range of motion); sport-specific outcomes were collected in less
than 15% of trials. Biomechanical, physiological, and neural/psychological outcomes were assessed sparsely and heteroge-
neously; only five trials investigated injury-related outcomes.
Conclusions There is room for improvement, with many areas of research on stretching being underexplored and others cur-
rently too heterogeneous for reliable comparisons between studies. There is limited representation of elite-level athletes (~ 5%
tier 4 and no tier 5) and underpowered sample sizes (≤ 20 participants). Research was biased toward adult male athletes of
sports not requiring extreme ranges of motion, and mostly assessed the acute effects of static active stretching and dynamic
stretching during the warm-up. Dose–response relationships remain largely underexplored. Outcomes were mostly limited
to general performance testing. Injury prevention and other effects of stretching remain poorly investigated. These relevant
research gaps should be prioritized by funding policies.

14	                                              After ACL Reconstruction?
15	                                              Reviewing the Criteria
16	                                              Yonatan Kaplan, PT, PhD,*† and Erik Witvrouw, PT, PhD‡
17	
18	                                              Context: There is an ever-increasing trend toward sports, fitness, and recreation activities, so the incidence of anterior
19	                                              cruciate ligament sports injuries has increased. Perhaps the greatest challenge for sports clinicians is to return the injured
20	                                              athlete back to his/her original sport at an even greater level of functional ability than preinjury. For this, rigorous and well-
21	                                              researched criteria are needed.
22	                                              Evidence Acquisition: Using medical subject headings and free-text words, an electronic search was conducted up to
23	                                              October 2018. Subject-specific search was based on the terms “return to play” and “return to sport” in combination with
24	                                              “guidelines,” “criteria,” and “anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.”
25	                                              Study Design: Descriptive review.
26	                                              Level of Evidence: Level 2.
27	                                              Results: Five principal criteria were found, including psychological factors, performance/functional tests, strength tests,
28	                                              time, and modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors.
29	                                              Conclusion: The psychological readiness of the player is a major factor in successful safe return to sport (SRTS) decision
30	                                              making. Although strength, performance, and functional tests presently form the mainstay of SRTS criteria, there exists very
31	                                              little scientific evidence for their validity. More protection should be provided to athletes with known risk factors. Movement
32	                                              quality is important, if not more important than the quantifiable measures. As a result of the significantly high rerupture rate
33	                                              in young individuals, delayed SRTS should be considered preferably beyond 9 months postsurgery.
34	                                              Keywords: ACL reconstruction; return to sport criteria; clinical decision making

                                              When Is It Safe to Return to Sport
                                              After ACL Reconstruction?
                                              Reviewing the Criteria
                                              Yonatan Kaplan, PT, PhD,*† and Erik Witvrouw, PT, PhD‡

                                              Context: There is an ever-increasing trend toward sports, fitness, and recreation activities, so the incidence of anterior
                                              cruciate ligament sports injuries has increased. Perhaps the greatest challenge for sports clinicians is to return the injured
                                              athlete back to his/her original sport at an even greater level of functional ability than preinjury. For this, rigorous and well-
                                              researched criteria are needed.
                                              Evidence Acquisition: Using medical subject headings and free-text words, an electronic search was conducted up to
                                              October 2018. Subject-specific search was based on the terms “return to play” and “return to sport” in combination with
                                              “guidelines,” “criteria,” and “anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.”
                                              Study Design: Descriptive review.
                                              Level of Evidence: Level 2.
                                              Results: Five principal criteria were found, including psychological factors, performance/functional tests, strength tests,
                                              time, and modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors.
                                              Conclusion: The psychological readiness of the player is a major factor in successful safe return to sport (SRTS) decision
                                              making. Although strength, performance, and functional tests presently form the mainstay of SRTS criteria, there exists very
                                              little scientific evidence for their validity. More protection should be provided to athletes with known risk factors. Movement
                                              quality is important, if not more important than the quantifiable measures. As a result of the significantly high rerupture rate
                                              in young individuals, delayed SRTS should be considered preferably beyond 9 months postsurgery.
                                              Keywords: ACL reconstruction; return to sport criteria; clinical decision making

                                                                             Although numerous risk factors may be modifiable, many are not.

                                                                             account when returning the injured athlete to sport. In some
                                                                             cases, added protection should be considered, for example adding
                                                                             rehabilitation time before returning the adolescent player to
                                                                             sport.35 What is of most concern is the evidence of increasing
                                                                             incidence of ACLR in younger patients.23,35,49 This is a growing
                                                                             public health burden and has potential ramifications for long-term
                                                                             health outcomes. Although 96% of young athletes are able to RTS

             In healthy athletes, the prescription of training load prioritises the development of sport-specific capacity to improve performance and minimise injury risk, but
             consideration of injury history is also important. In this respect, healthy athletes also benefit from loading to improve local tissue capacity. Conversely, the prescription of
             training load in injured athletes prioritises the development of local tissue loading to decrease pain and inhibition and increase function. However, local tissue loading in
             isolation, is insufficient to return injured athletes to competition. Scheduling training to emphasise the development of sport-specific capacity is required to bridge the
             gap between early stage rehabilitation and return to performance.
